before.content_html:
Electron Flow in Circuits

Electric current in a conductor is caused by the movement of electrons. In a metal wire, free electrons drift from the negative terminal of the supply towards the positive terminal — this is called electron flow. Conventional current, used in circuit diagrams and calculations, is defined as flowing from positive to negative, which is the opposite direction. For all OCR calculations you use conventional current direction, but you should be aware that actual electron flow goes the other way.

Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop. The same current flows through every component, but the supply voltage is shared between them. The total resistance of a series circuit is simply the sum of all individual resistances: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3. If three resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω, and 30 Ω are connected in series, the total resistance is 60 Ω.

In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two nodes. Every component receives the full supply voltage, and the total current is the sum of the currents through each branch. The total resistance of a parallel circuit is lower than any individual resistor. For two resistors: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2. For three resistors: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Always find 1/R_total first, then take the reciprocal to get R_total.

Key Fact

Series: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 (resistances add directly). Parallel (up to three resistors): 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 — always take the reciprocal of your final sum to get R_total. The OCR specification covers a maximum of three resistors in either configuration.

Ohm's Law: V = I × R

Ohm's law states that the potential difference across a component is directly proportional to the current through it, provided temperature is constant. The formula is V = I × R, where V is voltage in volts (V), I is current in amps (A), and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). You must be able to rearrange this formula: I = V ÷ R to find current; R = V ÷ I to find resistance. For example, if a resistor has 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A flows through it, its resistance is R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω.

Watt's Law: P = I × V

The power dissipated by a component equals the current through it multiplied by the voltage across it: P = I × V, where P is power in watts (W). This formula can be rearranged: I = P ÷ V; V = P ÷ I. For example, a motor operating at 6 V and drawing a current of 2 A has a power consumption of P = 2 × 6 = 12 W. Remove the sentence 'Note that OCR explicitly excludes P = I² × R from the specification — you only need P = I × V.' Replace with: 'P = I × V is the formula most directly tested; the derived forms P = I²R and P = V²/R can be used when voltage is not directly given — check your specification formula sheet to confirm which forms are supplied in the exam.'

Key Fact

Ohm's law: V = I × R (V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms). Watt's law: P = I × V (P in watts). Both formulas must be used with base units — convert any kΩ or mA to Ω or A before substituting. Remove 'OCR does not require P = I² × R.' Teach P = IV as primary; note that derived forms are also standard.

AC and DC: Types of Current

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only; its voltage remains constant over time. Batteries supply DC. Alternating current (AC) repeatedly reverses direction; the voltage rises and falls in a regular cycle. The UK mains supply is AC at 230 V, 50 Hz. Most electronic circuits use DC internally, but mains power is AC — a transformer and rectifier convert AC to DC in a mains adaptor.

Analogue and Digital Signals

An analogue signal varies continuously and can take any value within a range — like the output of a microphone or a temperature sensor. A digital signal takes only two discrete states: high (1) or low (0). The waveforms for these signals look very different: an analogue signal produces a smooth sine wave with a continuous range of amplitudes, while a digital signal produces a square wave that switches sharply between two voltage levels. Key waveform properties include: amplitude (the peak height of the wave), frequency (the number of complete cycles per second in Hz), and periodic time (the duration of one complete cycle, T = 1 ÷ f).

Three resistors — 10 Ω, 20 Ω, and 40 Ω — are connected in parallel. Find the total resistance. Step 1: 1/R_total = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/40 Step 2: Convert to a common denominator of 40: 4/40 + 2/40 + 1/40 = 7/40 Step 3: R_total = 40 ÷ 7 ≈ 5.71 Ω Notice that the total resistance (5.71 Ω) is less than the smallest individual resistor (10 Ω) — this is always true in a parallel circuit. Show all three steps in exam working to maximise method marks.

Analogue signals capture the full continuous range of a measurement, which can mean higher fidelity — a microphone output faithfully follows every nuance of sound. However, analogue signals are susceptible to noise: any interference adds to the signal and cannot easily be removed. Digital signals can be regenerated perfectly from their two-state nature — if a signal is noisy but clearly above the threshold, a circuit can restore it to a clean 1. Digital signals are also easier to process, store, and transmit reliably, which is why almost all modern communication and computing systems use digital formats. The trade-off is that converting from analogue to digital (via an ADC) introduces a small quantisation error — the continuous signal is approximated in discrete steps.

practice_questions.text:
A circuit contains two resistors connected in parallel: R1 = 12 Ω and R2 = 6 Ω. The supply voltage is 12 V.

Describe how to calculate the total resistance and use it to calculate the total current drawn from the supply.
practice_questions.marks:
Parallel resistance (2 marks): 1/R_total = 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/12 + 2/12 = 3/12; R_total = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω (1 mark for correct formula application; 1 mark for correct R_total = 4 Ω with unit).
Current calculation (2 marks): I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4; I = 3 A (1 mark for correct substitution; 1 mark for correct answer 3 A with unit). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing a portable LED torch. The torch uses two AA batteries (each 1.5 V) in series and the LED circuit draws a current of 20 mA.

Discuss the key circuit considerations the student should take into account when designing the torch.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): balanced discussion with at least two developed factors. For example: total supply voltage = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V; the student must calculate the series resistor needed to limit current to 20 mA — using V = I × R (with the voltage dropped across the resistor = supply voltage minus Change 'LED forward voltage ≈ 2 V if LED Vf ≈ 1 V, R = 2 ÷ 0.020 = 100 Ω' to 'LED forward voltage (Vf) for a typical red LED ≈ 2 V; voltage across resistor = 3 − 2 = 1 V; R = 1 ÷ 0.020 = 50 Ω (accept any value using a realistic Vf of 1.8–2.2 V with correct arithmetic)') — this prevents the LED from burning out (first factor, developed with calculation). Contrasted with: power consumption affects battery life — P = I × V = 0.020 × 3 = 0.06 W means the batteries will drain over time, so the student must consider capacity and efficiency in the design (second factor, developed with calculation and application to the scenario).
Secure (3–4 marks): two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): one factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): a single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A factory uses a 24 V DC motor to drive a conveyor belt. The motor has a resistance of 8 Ω and draws a current of 3 A at full load.

Evaluate the suitability of using direct current (DC) for this application compared to alternating current (AC), using your knowledge of circuit behaviour and calculations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): a balanced evaluation supported by calculations and application to the factory scenario. Arguments for DC: motors in control systems require a constant, predictable current direction — a DC motor's speed and torque are directly controllable via voltage (V = I × R gives 24 = 3 × 8 Ω, consistent with spec), and DC power P = I × V = 3 × 24 = 72 W is constant and predictable. DC from a battery/PSU also means the motor is independent of mains supply fluctuations. Arguments for AC consideration: mains supply is AC (230 V, 50 Hz) so the factory's power infrastructure is AC — powering a DC motor from AC requires a rectifier and voltage regulation circuit, adding complexity and cost. In high-power industrial applications, AC motors can be more robust and cheaper to maintain. Counter: for precision conveyor control, DC is widely preferred because speed can be varied by simply varying voltage; AC motor speed is fundamentally tied to mains frequency, requiring a frequency inverter to vary speed. A clear, substantiated judgement: DC is the more suitable choice for this precision, controlled-speed conveyor application, though it requires appropriate power conversion from the mains AC supply.
Secure (5–6 marks): arguments on both sides with calculations and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): relevant points with limited calculations, largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points, no evaluation or judgement. [8 marks]

before.content_html:
Programming a Programmable System

A programmable component such as a microcontroller does nothing useful until it is given a program — a precise sequence of instructions that tells it how to respond to inputs and control outputs. The specification identifies three types of programming language and system used to write or represent those instructions: text-based languages, block-based editors, and flowchart systems. Each has different characteristics, and the right choice depends on the complexity of the task and the experience of the programmer.

Text-Based Programming Languages

A text-based language requires the programmer to type instructions using the exact keywords and syntax of the chosen language — for example, C, MicroPython, or the Arduino language. Text-based code gives the greatest flexibility and control: any logic, however complex, can be expressed, and the resulting programs run efficiently on a microcontroller's processor. The disadvantage is the learning curve — syntax errors cause the program to fail, and beginners may find it hard to understand code written by others. Text-based code is the standard approach in professional and industrial engineering.

Key Fact

The three programming types are: text-based (written code, most powerful, steepest learning curve), block-based (drag-and-drop visual blocks, easier for beginners, limited for complex programs) and flowchart systems (visual symbols representing the flow of control, easy to plan and communicate, but can become complex to follow on large programs).

Block-Based Editors

Block-based editors such as Scratch or Microsoft MakeCode represent program instructions as graphical blocks that are dragged and snapped together on screen. Each block has a fixed shape that only allows valid connections, so syntax errors are almost impossible. This makes block-based editors highly accessible for beginners and for quickly prototyping simple control logic. The limitation is that complex logic quickly becomes cluttered and hard to follow, and not all programming concepts — particularly low-level hardware control — can be represented easily with pre-defined blocks. Block-based editors are widely used in schools and for rapid concept testing.

Text-based code transfers directly to professional and industrial settings — skills learned in Arduino C or Python are used in real engineering roles. Block-based editors, by contrast, are primarily educational tools. Some platforms such as MakeCode for the micro:bit allow the programmer to switch between block view and the equivalent text-based (Python or JavaScript) view of the same program, which helps learners make the transition. For the OCR exam, you need to understand the relative merits of each type and be able to argue which is more suitable for a given scenario — you are not expected to write actual code.

Flowchart Systems

A flowchart uses standardised shapes connected by arrows to represent the flow of control through a program. The key symbols are: an oval for start/end (terminal), a rectangle for a process step (such as 'turn LED on'), a diamond for a decision (a yes/no question), and a parallelogram for input or output. Flowchart software such as Flowol or PicLogicator can directly interpret a drawn flowchart as a program and run it on a connected programmable system. The advantage of flowcharts is that they make the logic of a program immediately visible, making them easy to plan, communicate, and debug. The disadvantage is that large, complex programs produce sprawling flowcharts that become difficult to read and maintain.

Key Fact

The four standard flowchart symbols are: oval — terminal (start/stop); rectangle — process (an action or calculation); diamond — decision (a yes/no question that creates a branch); parallelogram — input or output (e.g. reading a sensor or switching an output device). Arrows show the direction of flow between each step.

Using a Flowchart to Control a Programmable System

A flowchart directly models how a microcontroller or PLC executes a program. Consider a simple temperature alarm: the flowchart starts (oval), reads the temperature sensor (parallelogram — input), then reaches a decision diamond: 'Is temperature above 30°C?' If yes, an arrow leads to a process rectangle 'Turn on buzzer' and an output parallelogram; if no, an arrow loops back to read the sensor again. This loop continues indefinitely. The flowchart both communicates the design to other engineers and, in systems like Flowol, can be executed directly as the program itself. Identifying where decision diamonds create loops or branches is key to both drawing and interpreting flowcharts in the exam.

The choice of programming method depends on the experience of the programmer and the complexity of the task. For a beginner or for planning and communicating a simple control algorithm, flowcharts and block-based editors are the most accessible. For a complex, high-performance system that needs precise hardware control or efficient code, a text-based language is most appropriate. In an exam scenario question, always link your choice to the programmer's skill level, the complexity of the program required, and whether the code needs to be maintainable by others in a team.
before.exam_tip_html: Flowchart questions may ask you to complete, correct, or draw part of a flowchart. Always use the correct symbol shapes — drawing a process step as a diamond will lose marks. For 'compare' or 'discuss' questions about programming types, structure your answer around named advantages and disadvantages of each type, linked to the specific scenario in the question. A common mistake is describing what a flowchart looks like without explaining why the visual structure makes it easier to plan or debug a program compared with written code.

before.content_html:
Why Test a Circuit?

Building a prototype circuit is only worthwhile if the circuit is then tested methodically to confirm it behaves as designed. Testing reveals faults — incorrect voltages, broken connections, components that have failed — before the product is manufactured in quantity. The OCR specification lists five items of test equipment: the multimeter, the continuity tester, the oscilloscope, the signal generator, and the logic probe. Each instrument has specific uses, benefits, limitations, and safety requirements.

Multimeter

A multimeter measures DC voltage (in volts), DC current (in amps or milliamps), and resistance (in ohms). To measure voltage, the probes are placed across (in parallel with) the component. To measure current, the circuit must be broken and the multimeter inserted in series — the current flows through the meter. To measure resistance, the component must be disconnected from the circuit and no power applied. Safe use requires selecting the correct measurement function and range before connecting probes; measuring current without breaking the circuit or selecting the wrong range can damage the meter or cause a short circuit. Digital multimeters display a numerical reading and are more accurate and easier to read than analogue models. A multimeter cannot measure rapidly changing or high-frequency AC signals — an oscilloscope is needed for those.

Key Fact

A multimeter measures DC voltage (probes in parallel — across the component), current (probes in series — circuit broken, meter inserted), and resistance (component disconnected, no power). Always select the correct function and range before connecting. Never measure current without breaking the circuit first — this risks a dangerous short circuit through the meter.

Continuity Tester

A continuity tester checks whether a continuous electrical path exists between two points. When the probes are touched to either end of a wire, track, or connection, the tester beeps (or lights an LED) if current can flow. It is the quickest way to identify a broken wire, a lifted PCB track, or a faulty switch. Safety requirement: the circuit must be powered off before testing — applying continuity probes to a live circuit risks damaging the tester and causing a short. A continuity tester cannot measure voltage or resistance values; it only confirms presence or absence of a path.

Oscilloscope

An oscilloscope displays voltage plotted against time, showing the actual waveform of a signal on its screen. Unlike a multimeter, it can capture rapidly changing signals — both AC sine waves and digital square waves — and measure their amplitude (peak voltage), frequency, and periodic time (the time for one complete cycle). This makes it essential for testing audio circuits, timing circuits, and any system where signal shape matters. Probes are connected in parallel across the point to be measured. An oscilloscope is more complex to set up than a multimeter and more expensive; it does not directly measure resistance or DC current. Safety: use probes with the correct voltage rating for the signal being measured.

The oscilloscope screen is divided into a grid. The vertical axis (Y) represents voltage — each division represents a set number of volts (the volts/div setting). The horizontal axis (X) represents time — each division represents a set time period (the time/div setting). To find amplitude, count the vertical divisions from the lowest to highest point of the wave and multiply by the volts/div. To find the period (time for one cycle), count the horizontal divisions for one complete wave cycle and multiply by the time/div. Frequency equals one divided by the period (f = 1/T). In the OCR exam you may be asked to read values from an oscilloscope display — practise counting grid squares carefully.

Signal Generator and Logic Probe

A signal generator is used alongside the oscilloscope: it produces a controllable electrical signal — sine, square, or other waveform — at a chosen frequency and amplitude, which is fed into the circuit under test. This allows the engineer to check how the circuit responds to specific input signals without needing a live sensor. A logic probe is a simple pen-shaped tool used specifically on digital circuits. Touching its tip to a point in the circuit lights a high LED (logic 1) or a low LED (logic 0), instantly revealing the state of a digital signal. It cannot measure analogue voltage levels but is faster and cheaper than an oscilloscope for basic digital circuit checking.

Key Fact

Five test instruments: multimeter (DC voltage, current, resistance — general purpose); continuity tester (checks for unbroken electrical path — must be used on a powered-off circuit); oscilloscope (displays waveform, measures amplitude and frequency); signal generator (produces a controlled test signal to feed into a circuit); logic probe (shows logic high or low on digital circuits — simple and fast).

A systematic approach to fault-finding follows a logical order. First, visually inspect the circuit for obvious problems: solder bridges, components in the wrong orientation, or damaged tracks. Second, check the power supply with a multimeter — confirm correct voltage is reaching the circuit. Third, use a continuity tester to verify all intended connections are complete. Fourth, work through the circuit stage by stage: measure the voltage at the output of each section (input stage, processing stage, output stage) and compare it with the expected value. Fifth, if signals are involved, use an oscilloscope to verify waveform shapes at key nodes. Replacing a suspected faulty component is the last step after the fault has been narrowed down logically, not the first step.

From Prototype to Printed Circuit Board

Once a circuit design has been validated on a breadboard or stripboard prototype, the next step in commercial production is to manufacture a printed circuit board (PCB). A PCB replaces the hand-wired connections of a prototype with precise copper tracks that are reproduced identically on every board, reducing errors and enabling mass manufacture. The OCR specification covers two production methods — photo etching and CAM milling/routing — and three types of PCB: single-sided, double-sided, and flexible.

Photo Etching

Photo etching (also called the photochemical process or UV etching) uses ultraviolet light and a chemical etchant to transfer a track pattern onto a copper-clad board. The process has several distinct stages. First, the PCB layout is printed as a positive or negative image onto a transparent film (the photomask). Second, the copper-clad board — coated with a UV-sensitive layer called photoresist — is placed under the photomask and exposed to UV light. Where the UV light reaches the photoresist it hardens (or softens, depending on whether positive or negative resist is used). Third, a developer chemical removes the unexposed (soft) photoresist, leaving the hardened photoresist protecting only the intended copper tracks. Fourth, the board is immersed in an etchant solution — typically ferric chloride or ammonium persulphate — which dissolves all exposed copper, leaving only the copper beneath the protective resist. Fifth, the remaining photoresist is stripped away to reveal the finished copper tracks. Finally, holes are drilled for through-hole components. Photo etching produces very fine, accurate tracks and is the dominant method in commercial PCB production.

Key Fact

The five stages of photo etching are: (1) print photomask; (2) UV exposure — UV light hardens the photoresist over the track pattern; (3) develop — remove unexposed resist; (4) etch — dissolve unprotected copper in etchant chemical; (5) strip remaining resist to reveal copper tracks. Etchant chemicals are hazardous — proper safety precautions (gloves, goggles, neutralisation and disposal) are always required.

CAM Milling/Routing

CAM milling (Computer-Aided Manufacture milling or routing) uses a CNC (computer numerically controlled) machine fitted with a small cutting bit to physically remove copper from a copper-clad board. The PCB design file is sent directly to the milling machine, which follows the track outlines precisely, cutting away the copper between tracks so that only the desired conductive paths remain. The advantages of CAM milling are that no chemicals are required (making it safer and more environmentally friendly), it produces a board very quickly from a design file, and it is well-suited to school or workshop use for one-off prototype PCBs. The disadvantages are that the track resolution is coarser than photo etching (minimum track spacing is limited by the cutter size), and the process is slower and less cost-effective for large-volume production than photo etching.

Photo etching is favoured for commercial mass production because it can produce very fine tracks (important for densely packed components), is fast for large batches, and the same photomask can be reused to make hundreds of identical boards. CAM milling is favoured for low-quantity, rapid-prototyping situations — particularly in schools and small engineering workshops — because there are no hazardous chemicals involved, no need for a darkroom or UV exposure unit, and the board is ready almost immediately after the CNC program finishes. For an exam question comparing the two, always link your choice to the scale of production and the track resolution required.

Types of PCB: Single-Sided

A single-sided PCB has copper tracks on one side of the insulating board only. Components are mounted on the opposite (component) side and their leads pass through holes to be soldered to the tracks underneath. Single-sided boards are the simplest and cheapest to manufacture. They are suitable for circuits that are not very complex — where all the routing can be achieved without tracks needing to cross. Their limitation is that complex circuits cannot be routed on a single side without track crossovers, which are not possible without bridges or additional wiring.

Key Fact

Three PCB types: single-sided (copper one side — cheapest, suits simple circuits); double-sided (copper both sides — suits complex circuits, can use vias to connect layers); flexible (copper tracks on thin flexible substrate — suits wearables and curved enclosures, but more expensive and harder to manufacture).

Types of PCB: Double-Sided and Flexible

A double-sided PCB has copper tracks on both sides of the board. Connections between the two layers are made through small plated holes called vias. Double-sided boards greatly increase the routing density that can be achieved — complex circuits such as microcontroller development boards and motor controllers are typically double-sided. The manufacturing process is more involved (both sides must be etched and aligned precisely), and cost is higher than single-sided. A flexible PCB uses a thin, flexible polymer substrate rather than the rigid fibreglass (FR4) of standard boards, allowing the circuit to bend, fold, or conform to a curved surface. Flexible PCBs are used in products where space is very restricted or the board must flex during use — for example, inside a fold-up phone, a camera module, or a wearable health monitor. They are more expensive to manufacture than rigid boards and can be damaged by repeated sharp bending.

The choice of PCB type is driven by circuit complexity, product form factor, and budget. If the circuit is simple (such as a basic LED driver or a small sensor module) and cost is a priority, a single-sided PCB is appropriate. If the circuit is complex — many components, dense interconnections — a double-sided PCB allows the routing to be split between layers. If the product must fit inside a curved or flexible enclosure, or the circuit board itself must flex during use (such as a fitness tracker wristband), a flexible PCB is required despite its higher cost. In exam answers, always justify your chosen PCB type with a specific reason linked to the product scenario.

A) Photo etching
B) UV exposure
C) CAM milling/routing

practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: no hazardous chemicals needed / safer for students to use / produces the board quickly from a design file / no need for a UV exposure unit or darkroom / more environmentally friendly as no chemical waste is produced. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a double-sided PCB would be chosen over a single-sided PCB for a complex microcontroller-based circuit.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a double-sided PCB has tracks on both sides'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'having copper tracks on both sides of the board significantly increases the routing density — connections that cannot be routed on a single layer can be run on the opposite side'). A further developed point scores 3 marks (e.g. adding 'the two layers are connected where needed using plated through-holes called vias, allowing very complex circuits with many interconnections to be fitted onto a compact board that would be impossible to route on a single side'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stage of photo etching in which etchant is used. Include what the etchant does and one safety precaution that must be followed.
practice_questions.marks: Description of etching stage (up to 2 marks): after development, the board is immersed in an etchant solution such as ferric chloride, which chemically dissolves the copper that is not protected by the hardened photoresist, leaving only the copper tracks beneath the resist (2 marks for a full description identifying the chemical action; 1 mark for a basic statement). Safety precaution (up to 2 marks): gloves and goggles must be worn at all times when handling etchant chemicals as they are corrosive and can cause skin and eye damage; waste etchant must be neutralised and disposed of according to local safety regulations (2 marks for a specific, developed precaution; 1 mark for a vague statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is designing a new smart fitness wristband that must have an extremely thin and light circuit board that can flex with the wearer's wrist.

Discuss which type of PCB and which production method would be most suitable for this product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion recommending a flexible PCB for the wristband (justifying with specific reasons: thin polymer substrate allows the board to flex with the wrist; suitable for wearable products where rigid boards would snap or cause discomfort) and then discussing the production method — photo etching is more suitable than CAM milling for the fine tracks needed on a compact flexible board, even though chemicals are required. Acknowledges at least one limitation of flexible PCB (higher cost, more complex manufacture, can crack with repeated sharp bending). Both aspects developed and linked to the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): PCB type correctly identified with a justification and some discussion of production method.
Developing (2 marks): Correct PCB type named with a basic reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A PCB type named with no justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which photo etching is a more suitable PCB production method than CAM milling for all types of circuit production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies clear strengths of photo etching (very fine track resolution, fast for large batches, photomask reused for identical boards, industry standard) and then challenges these with well-developed counter-arguments where CAM milling is more suitable (no hazardous chemicals, safer, faster for a single prototype, no UV equipment needed, accessible in schools and small workshops). Considers specific scenarios — for example, mass-producing a consumer product (photo etching better) vs producing one prototype PCB in a school (CAM milling better). Reaches a substantiated conclusion that photo etching is not universally more suitable and is at a clear disadvantage for one-off or small-scale production. Judgement is clearly stated and supported.
Secure (5-6 marks): Strengths and limitations identified with some comparison and a partial judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points listed but limited comparison; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic description of one method with little evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which chemical is typically used in the photo etching process to dissolve unprotected copper from the board?
Which type of PCB uses a thin polymer substrate that allows it to bend and flex?

before.content_html:
From PCB to Finished Circuit

Producing the bare PCB is only the first half of circuit manufacture. The second half is circuit assembly — mounting components onto the board and creating reliable electrical connections between them. The OCR specification identifies three assembly methods: surface mount technology (SMT), through-hole construction, and manual soldering. Each has distinct characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages, and the right choice depends on the scale of production, the components used, and the application.

Surface Mount Technology (SMT)

Surface mount technology (SMT) is the dominant method in modern commercial electronics manufacture. SMT components have no wire leads — instead, they have small metal terminations on their bodies that sit directly on copper pads on the surface of the PCB. Two automated processes are used: first, solder paste (a mixture of tiny solder particles and flux) is printed onto the pads using a stencil. Then, a pick and place machine uses vacuum nozzles to pick individual components from reels or trays at high speed and place them precisely onto the solder paste. Replace 'this is called reflow soldering' with 'this is called reflow soldering' SMT allows very compact circuit layouts (components are much smaller than through-hole equivalents), very high assembly speeds, and both sides of a PCB to be populated. The disadvantages are that SMT components are extremely small and difficult to handle or solder by hand; specialised, expensive equipment is required; and reworking or replacing individual components is more challenging than with through-hole parts.

Key Fact

SMT assembly has two automated stages: (1) pick and place — a robotic machine places tiny components onto solder paste printed on the PCB pads; Replace '(2) reflow soldering — the board passes through a reflow oven' with '(2) reflow soldering — the board passes through a reflow oven' SMT advantage: very compact, fast, suited to mass production. SMT disadvantage: components are too small to solder by hand; expensive automated equipment is required.

Through-Hole Construction

Through-hole construction uses components with wire leads that are pushed through holes drilled in the PCB and soldered to copper pads on the underside. Through-hole components are physically larger than SMT equivalents and create mechanically very strong joints — the lead passing through the board provides a physical anchor. This makes through-hole construction suitable for components that experience mechanical stress, vibration, or repeated connection/disconnection — for example, connectors, power transistors, large capacitors, and switches. Through-hole assembly is also far easier to carry out by hand, making it the standard approach in schools, repair workshops, and for prototyping. The disadvantages are that the holes occupy board space on both layers, limiting routing density, and the components are bulkier, preventing the same miniaturisation achievable with SMT.

Modern commercial electronics predominantly use SMT because the small component size allows smartphones, laptops, and wearables to be as compact as they are. However, through-hole components are still found even on modern PCBs — particularly for connectors (USB ports, power sockets), high-power components (large electrolytic capacitors, power MOSFETs), and mechanical mounting points that benefit from a physically anchored joint. A PCB that uses both SMT and through-hole components is called a mixed-technology board. For the OCR exam, always compare the two based on size, mechanical strength, ease of manual assembly, and suitability for mass production.

Manual Soldering

Manual soldering involves a technician using a soldering iron (typically heated to between 320°C and 380°C) and solder wire to join component leads to PCB pads by hand. The iron tip heats both the component lead and the pad simultaneously; solder wire is then fed into the joint, melts, and flows around the heated surfaces. When the iron is removed, the solder cools and solidifies, creating both an electrical and a mechanical connection. A good solder joint is shiny, smooth, and volcano-shaped. A poor joint — called a cold (dry) joint — is dull, grainy, and has high resistance. Manual soldering is used for through-hole prototyping, repair work, and assembly of low-volume or bespoke circuits. It is unsuitable for SMT components at the normal production scale because the components are too small and the process is too slow for mass manufacture. Safety: the iron tip reaches temperatures that cause immediate burns — always use a stand, avoid touching the tip, and work in a ventilated area to avoid inhaling flux fumes.

Key Fact

Three assembly methods: SMT (tiny surface-mounted components, pick-and-place + reflow oven, mass production — but expensive equipment and difficult to hand-solder); through-hole (leads through drilled holes, strong mechanical joint, easy to hand-solder — but larger components, less dense layout); manual soldering (hand-applied with soldering iron, used for prototypes and repairs — but slow, requires skill, unsuitable for SMT at scale).

A good solder joint must be electrically conductive, mechanically secure, and resistant to fracture in use. In practice, a well-made through-hole joint should be shiny (indicating the solder flowed and bonded correctly), smooth, and volcano-shaped — broader at the pad and tapering up the component lead. A cold joint forms when the pad or lead is insufficiently heated before solder is applied; the solder solidifies before flowing properly, leaving a dull, crumbly surface and a high-resistance connection that may fail intermittently. Other defects include solder bridges (solder accidentally connecting two adjacent pads, causing a short circuit) and insufficient solder (leaving a weak joint). Visual inspection under magnification is the primary quality check for manual soldering in a workshop environment.

Key Takeaways

  • SMT places tiny components on PCB surface pads using a Replace 'reflow soldering in a reflow oven' with 'reflow soldering in a reflow oven' — it is fast and compact but requires expensive automated equipment.
  • Through-hole construction threads component leads through drilled holes and solders them on the underside — the joints are strong and easy to make by hand, but the components are larger and use more board space.
  • Manual soldering with a heated iron is used for prototyping, repairs, and low-volume assembly of through-hole components; a good joint is shiny and smooth, while a cold (dry) joint is dull, grainy, and electrically unreliable.
